title: Cognitive Coaching: Changing Minds and Changing Practice
author: Sarah Cottinghatt
summary: In the debut post of her Cognitive Coaching newsletter, Sarah Cottinghatt argues that instructional coaching has focused heavily on building teachers' knowledge and technique repertoire but has neglected the third link in the chain: judgement, the ability to select the right action at the right time for the right reason. She grounds judgement in the concept of mental models, simplified internal representations of 'how things work' that let people interpret complex situations and act, illustrating with research showing that landscapers, taxonomists, and maintenance workers categorise the same trees completely differently depending on their mental models. She explains that expert teachers' mental models let them run mental simulations, predicting how an action will play out before taking it, using an example of a teacher sensing a discussion question will be too hard and adjusting on the fly. Because mental models are tacit and rarely examined directly, Cottinghatt argues coaching's real job is to help teachers surface, examine, and deliberately revise their models, not just drill techniques, a practice she names 'cognitive coaching' after this newsletter. She closes by previewing future posts on the specific tools she uses to develop teacher mental models in her coaching practice.
points: Cottinghatt argues coaching typically builds knowledge and technique well but neglects the third link, judgement, the capacity to choose the right action at the right time for the right reason.

She grounds judgement in mental models, tacit internal representations that filter what a person notices and how they interpret a situation, illustrated by how differently landscapers and taxonomists categorise the same trees.
She explains that expert mental models allow real-time simulation, mentally 'running' the likely effect of an action before taking it, which lets skilled teachers adjust mid-lesson.
Her core coaching claim is that because mental models are tacit, coaching's real job is surfacing and revising them explicitly, not just reinforcing observable techniques.
quotes: knowledge/experience -> judgement -> action. I think we are pretty good at helping teachers build knowledge... but I don't think we are good (yet) at supporting teachers to develop their judgement.
It also strikes me that if we skip the 'judgement' part of teaching, we are ignoring the very thing that makes a teacher a professional.
Mental models are a construct. Put very simply, they are our knowledge of 'how things work.' They simplify complex situations enabling us to interpret them and act.
Everyone's mental models are different even about similar, simple things, like trees.
Because mental models contain causal relationships, they can be simulated, i.e. we can press play and 'run' what might happen if we do something.

Our mental models are tacit. It's rare we actually examine our mental models rather than just think with them. This is why it's so important for coaches to focus their work on helping the teacher surface their mental models.
Expertise is the ability to do the thing that works most of the time and to know when and how to adapt. It's about recognising 'decision points.'
